data.title: Picsart Opens the AI Behind Its Platform to Developers & Businesses
data.description:
Picsart Opens the AI Behind Its Platform to Developers & Businesses

With Picsart Platform, developers can build their own video, audio, image features using 250+ models from 30+ providers, alongside Picsart's own editing models, through one API, CLI or MCP server.

Key Takeaways

  • One bundle, four ways to build: the API, the CLI, a playground to test models, and Picsart Media Studio, an MCP server that works with compatible AI assistants.
  • One integration for image, video, audio and text generation from 250+ models across 30+ providers, with the freedom to switch models as a product evolves. Self-serve users pay per generation at competitive, published rates.
  • Developers get access to Picsart's proprietary editing models, like Enhance and background removal, which are only available on Picsart Platform.

Picsart, the AI media production and distribution platform backed by Sequoia Capital and SoftBank Vision Fund 2, today launched Picsart Platform - a multimodal creative AI hub that gives developers the technology behind the platform used by more than 100 million people each month.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261120520968/en/

Picsart Opens the AI Behind Its Platform to Developers & Businesses. They can now build their own video, audio, image features using 250+ models from 30+ providers, alongside Picsart's own editing models, through one API, CLI or MCP server.

As new video and image models launch every few weeks, managing separate APIs, API keys, and billing systems creates a fragmented ecosystem. By offering unified access to creative tools, Picsart Platform eliminates fragmentation for all creators, spanning independent developers and corporate marketing teams and studios, by providing access to over 250 video, audio, image, and text models across 30+ providers through a unified integration. Picsart provides access to the latest models at launch, so users can try the newest one without rebuilding.

Developers can switch video models without rewriting their integration, and they can use Picsart's editing models to refine images before or after generation. Developers can access the entire catalog via REST API, Python and TypeScript SDKs, a CLI, or an MCP server. As teams increasingly rely on AI coding agents, having access to an MCP server becomes essential for seamless development.

Hovhannes Avoyan, Founder and CEO of Picsart, says: "Generative media is moving faster than any team can integrate it, our job is to keep up so our customers don't have to. Picsart Platform puts the newest creative AI models and Picsart's own editing tools within reach for solo developers, entrepreneurs and the enterprises we're increasingly built to serve. A two-person startup and a global brand should have access to the same creative engine."

Launch Offer and Availability

Picsart Platform is officially live today. New users can access unlimited Wan 3.0 via Picsart Platform from November 20–22, there will also be an opportunity to receive bonus credits while the promotional pool remains available.

Get your API key at picsart.com/api-platform.

About Picsart

Picsart is the AI-powered platform built for a content-first world. For more than 14 years, it has empowered the next generation of storytellers to create, scale and now monetize video content. Combining intuitive design tools, AI-powered image and video creation, and MCP and CLI functions, Picsart meets creators wherever they work. With more than 100 million monthly active users and over 2.5 billion downloads to date, Picsart is powering a new era of scalable, self-directed creativity, where content fuels identity, influence, and entrepreneurship.

data.title: ASHLEY GIBSON BARNETT MUSEUM OF ART AT FLORIDA SOUTHERN COLLEGE PRESENTS LIFE: SIX WOMEN PHOTOGRAPHERS
data.description:
ASHLEY GIBSON BARNETT MUSEUM OF ART AT FLORIDA SOUTHERN COLLEGE PRESENTS LIFE: SIX WOMEN PHOTOGRAPHERS

ASHLEY GIBSON BARNETT MUSEUM OF ART AT FLORIDA SOUTHERN COLLEGE PRESENTS LIFE: SIX WOMEN PHOTOGRAPHERS

PR Newswire

LAKELAND, Fla., Nov. 20, 2026

LAKELAND, Fla., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Ashley Gibson Barnett Museum of Art (The AGB) at Florida Southern College is proud to present LIFE: Six Women Photographers, an exhibition celebrating six pioneering women whose groundbreaking work helped shape modern photojournalism and transformed how Americans experienced the world through photography. Featuring more than 70 photographs by Margaret Bourke-White, Marie Hansen, Martha Holmes, Lisa Larsen, Nina Leen and Hansel Mieth, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, 2026, and will remain on view through March 7, 2027.

The exhibition, organized by The New-York Historical Society, highlights the contributions of the only six women employed as full-time photographers by LIFE magazine between the late 1930s and early 1970s out of 101 photographers on staff during its run as a weekly publication. At a time when photojournalism was largely dominated by men, these photographers documented defining moments in American history, captured significant social and political changes, and brought compelling human stories to millions of readers.

"These six remarkable women helped shape the way generations of Americans experienced and understood the world through photography," said Dr. Daryl Ward, executive director of The AGB. "Their work not only documented pivotal moments in history but also challenged conventions in a profession where women were often overlooked. We are proud to bring this important exhibition to Central Florida and share their extraordinary contributions to photography and journalism with our community."

First presented in New York in 2019, the exhibition explores the way Americans saw the world through the lens of photographers at LIFE, the first magazine in the United States to tell stories with images rather than text. These innovative photo essays became the hallmark of the publication. The exhibition provides context to this unique storytelling format through published and unpublished photographs, including vintage prints, copy prints and contact sheets. In addition, the photographs show the editing process behind the final published stories that helped define the United States as a world power during what Henry Luce, LIFE founder and editor-in-chief, called the "American Century." This is the first exhibition to focus on the six women who worked as full-time photographers for LIFE.

LIFE: Six Women Photographers was curated by Marilyn Satin Kushner, former curator and head of the Department of Prints, Photographs, and Architectural Collections, as well as Sarah Gordon, curatorial scholar in women's history, with Erin Levitsky of Ryerson University and William J. Simmons, former Andrew Mellon Foundation Pre-Doctoral Fellow at the Center for Women's History.

The exhibition is proudly sponsored by Northern Trust. Generous support is provided by Joyce B. Cowin, with additional support from Lara Lee Schupf, Jerry Speyer, and Robert A.M. Stern. This exhibition has been organized by The New-York Historical Society.

LIFE is the registered trademark of TI Gotham Inc. Used under license.

data.title: Stocks could face a 'doom loop' if Wall Street underestimates the risk of an economic downturn, strategist warns
data.description:
By Steve Goldstein

Wall Street is underpricing the hard-landing risk, one Bank of America strategist says. Here's what investors should know.

A hard landing could trigger a "doom loop" for stocks, warns one Wall Street strategist.

The S&P 500 is nearing a level worth buying if the U.S. avoids a recession, but one strategist warns Wall Street is underpricing the risk of a hard landing, saying investors should wait before buying risky assets.

Strategists led by Michael Hartnett said if the Fed is still Wall Street's best friend and corporate credit and the S&P 500 continue to slide, market turmoil will "short-circuit" the Fed rate-hike cycle. But if the Fed is now an "inflation tough guy" after the midterms, the hard-landing risks grow.

Hartnett's comments come amid increasingly hawkish central-bank commentary, with St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem talking of the need for as many as four rate increases by the spring. Fed governor Christopher Waller has said the central bank should consider a half-point rate rise in December.

An S&P 500 SPX below 7,000, in a soft-landing scenario where the U.S. avoids a recession, would be a buy, he said.

The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,175.83, now more than 2% below its 200-day average. Stock-market futures (ES00) pointed to a weaker start on Friday.

Bank of America's own fund-manager survey, released Tuesday, showed half the investors they polled thought there would be a soft landing and 42% expected no landing at all, i.e. continued or accelerating growth. Only 3% expected a recession. "We say hard landing likelihood too low," said Hartnett.

He said he fears a doom loop, where once estimates of GDP and earnings per share are reduced, stock-market allocations are cut, and investors only sell what they own. For now, investors are "hiding" in low-volatility and defensive stocks, he said.

Investors should wait until the narrative flips from Fed hikes to Fed cuts, then buy "cyclicals Cs" - crypto, chips, copper, consumer and condos.

-Steve Goldstein

data.title: Williams CEO Chad Zamarin Urges House Action Following Senate Passage of Bipartisan Permitting Reform
data.description:
Williams CEO Chad Zamarin Urges House Action Following Senate Passage of Bipartisan Permitting Reform

Chad Zamarin, President and CEO of Williams (NYSE: WMB) released the following statement following the U.S. Senate’s passing of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026:

“The Senate’s passage of BAAJA is an important win for American families and American energy, and now the House has an opportunity to finish the job. We thank Senators Capito, Lee, Heinrich and Whitehouse for working together to advance meaningful, bipartisan permitting reform.

America has the energy, the resources and the capital to build. What we’ve lacked is a permitting system that lets us get it done. The BAAJA can change that, helping deliver the infrastructure we need to lower costs and meet rapidly growing energy demand.

Nowhere is that problem clearer than in the Northeast. During last winter’s cold snap, energy prices in New England spiked by more than 10 times the normal cost because the region simply does not have enough infrastructure to reliably access abundant and affordable American energy. Projects that could help solve that problem have been delayed or blocked for years.

BAAJA takes an important step toward lowering costs for Americans by bringing greater certainty and accountability to the permitting process. That means getting critical energy infrastructure built, strengthening reliability and helping lower energy bills for American families.

We urge the House to act quickly, pass BAAJA and get America back to building.”

About Williams

Williams (NYSE: WMB) is a trusted energy industry leader committed to safely, reliably and responsibly meeting growing energy demand. We use our infrastructure to deliver one third of the nation’s natural gas to where it's needed most, supplying the energy used to heat our homes, cook our food and generate low-carbon electricity. For over a century, we’ve been driven by a passion for doing things the right way. Today, our team of problem solvers is leading the charge into the clean energy future. data.title: Brayton Purcell Attorney Featured in San Francisco Chronicle Opinion Backing California Artificial Stone Ban, Calling on Other States to Follow
data.description:
Brayton Purcell Attorney Featured in San Francisco Chronicle Opinion Backing California Artificial Stone Ban, Calling on Other States to Follow

Brayton Purcell Attorney Featured in San Francisco Chronicle Opinion Backing California Artificial Stone Ban, Calling on Other States to Follow

PR Newswire

NOVATO, Calif., Nov. 20, 2026

Brayton Purcell LLP Partner James Nevin warns that artificial stone silicosis cases may be dramatically underreported nationwide as California moves toward prohibiting high-silica artificial stone

NOVATO, Calif., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- California is moving to prohibit the fabrication and manufacture of high-silica artificial stone, a countertop material linked to the growing silicosis crisis among fabrication workers.

A November 19 San Francisco Chronicle Open Forum article by health reporter Kayla Yup argues that California is taking the right approach and urges other states to follow its lead.

The opinion article, "California could soon ban engineered stone countertops. Here's why it should," examines the devastating health consequences affecting workers who fabricate artificial stone and the growing effort to prevent future cases.

California's Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board voted in May to begin the process of prohibiting the fabrication and installation of artificial stone products containing more than 1% crystalline silica. Cal/OSHA has developed rules addressing the manufacture and fabrication of these products.

Artificial Stone Silicosis Is an Ongoing Crisis

Artificial stone, also referred to as engineered or manufactured stone, is widely used for kitchen and bathroom countertops. The material is at least 90% respirable crystalline silica, with the remaining approximately 10% consisting of highly toxic dyes, resins, and heavy metals.

When artificial stone is cut, ground, or polished, fabrication produces nano-sized, high-surface-area respirable crystalline silica dust. The other components release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during fabrication.

In her San Francisco Chronicle article, Yup emphasizes the exceptionally high silica content of artificial stone: "Engineered stone contains more than 90% silica content. That's double the amount in granite and more than 18 times that of marble."

Workers fabricating these countertops inhale this highly toxic dust. Artificial stone silicosis is preventable, progressive, incurable, and fatal.

Yup illustrates the consequences through the experience of a 35-year-old Los Angeles countertop worker she identifies as Luis Hernandez, a pseudonym used because of his immigration status. When she first met him in February 2024, Yup writes that "he could not walk more than 50 feet without gasping for air."

Hernandez underwent a double-lung transplant in December 2024. His experience illustrates the profound and lasting consequences artificial stone silicosis has on workers and their families.

James Nevin Warns Silicosis Cases May Be Going Undetected Across the U.S.

The San Francisco Chronicle article examines California's comparatively robust silicosis surveillance efforts and raises concerns that the disease may be significantly underreported in other parts of the country.

As part of her reporting, Yup spoke with James Nevin, a partner and trial attorney at Brayton Purcell LLP, about the potential national scope of the crisis and the cases he is pursuing on behalf of affected workers and families.

Yup writes, "James Nevin, a lawyer spearheading hundreds of lawsuits against manufacturers, told me he estimates other states are missing 90% of workplace silicosis cases simply because they lack mandatory reporting."

According to the article, Nevin represents workers with silicosis and loved ones of workers who have died from the disease in approximately 22 states.

The figures raise an alarming possibility: California may not necessarily have a uniquely high number of affected workers. Rather, its surveillance program is identifying cases that remain undetected elsewhere.

California has documented an increasing number of silicosis cases associated with artificial stone fabrication. As of the date of publication, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) reports 697 artificial stone silicosis cases, 77 lung transplants and another 55 patients referred for a transplant. Approximately 98% of California workers diagnosed with silicosis associated with the industry are Latino men, and the average age of workers who have died from the disease is only 52.

"California is showing the rest of the country the true scope of this crisis," said Nevin. "If other states are not actively identifying these cases, sick workers remain invisible. California's action against high-silica artificial stone is an important step, but this disease does not stop at the state line."

California's Action Should Set an Example

California's proposed action would put the state at the forefront of efforts in the United States to address the dangers associated with fabricating high-silica artificial stone.

Australia prohibited artificial stone in 2024 after confronting its own silicosis crisis among countertop fabrication workers.

Yup argues that California should now move forward with its proposed prohibition, and that other states should learn from California's experience.

The need for action is underscored by workers who have already lost their lives. The Chronicle article describes a countertop fabrication worker who died from silicosis at age 41. In August, a Santa Monica jury assessed $47 million in favor of his family in litigation involving his artificial stone silicosis.

For Nevin and Brayton Purcell LLP, the implications extend well beyond California. If significant numbers of artificial stone silicosis cases are going undetected in states without comparable surveillance, the workers identified to date could represent only a small portion of the true national toll.

As Yup concludes, California cannot reverse the hundreds of artificial stone silicosis cases that have already been diagnosed. But prohibiting the product would prevent more workers from suffering the same fate, while giving other states a path to follow.

About Brayton Purcell LLP

Brayton Purcell LLP represents workers and families affected by artificial stone silicosis and is pursuing litigation against manufacturers and distributors of artificial stone products.

If you or a loved one developed silicosis after cutting, grinding, or polishing artificial stone countertops, you may have legal rights against companies involved in manufacturing and distributing these products.

Contact Brayton Purcell LLP to learn more about your legal options.

data.title: The Fed is too busy fighting inflation to rescue the stock market
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Concern about financial condition seems to favor a gradual pace of rate hikes

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at his press conference in October.

The U.S. stock market plunged this week into correction territory, with the major indexes down more than 10% from recent highs, but don't expect the U.S. central bank to come to the rescue.

Federal Reserve officials will continue to raise interest rates, despite the recent selloff in the stock market, as equity-market gains over the past four years dwarf the recent declines, economists said Friday.

"We would need a much larger retreat in equity values to make a dent in the wealth that has been generated by the stock market over the prior few years," said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist of CIBC Capital Markets.

Scott Anderson, chief U.S. economist at BMO Capital Markets agreed: "People have done so well over the past several years. There is some room for stocks to fall without all consumers stopping spending and air traffic going down."

Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said most Fed officials are looking through the stock-market volatility.

"Regardless of the fact that financial conditions have tightened, they will still want to signal and implement a tighter monetary stance," Daco said.

The Fed raised rates a quarter-point in September, the first increase in three years, in an effort to battle the persistent upward creep of consumer prices.

Officials made no change to rates in October, in part because the stock market was weak, according to minutes of the Fed meeting released Wednesday. At the same time, almost all Fed officials anticipated further rate hikes.

CIBC's Shenfeld said there are two reasons why stocks would matter for the Fed: if the market falls far enough to cause negative wealth effects, or if the market is a predictor of where the economy is going.

That's less likely to be true after the huge run-up of the past few years, he said.

"At this point, I don't think it is material for them. It can become material, but we're not there yet," Shenfeld added. The S&P 500 SPX is clinging to positive gains in 2026 and has returned 100% over the past four years.

Fed officials are focused on the risks to the economy and markets from a reversal of optimism surrounding AI. Minutes of their October meeting disclosed that officials had lengthy discussions over various scenarios surrounding a possible market selloff.

"They are starting to get serious about what their playbook would be if this would get worse," Anderson said. The biggest worry would be "systemic dislocation" in financial markets, he added.

That might require the Fed to set up special credit lines to inject liquidity into markets, similar to actions taken in the financial crisis of 2008 and the dawn of the COVID pandemic in 2020, Anderson said.

At the moment, the Fed might be breathing "a sigh of relief" over the recent stock-market drop because it is concerned about high stock valuations and related hedge-fund leverage. A modest decline in equities "lets some the air out of the balloon," Anderson said.

Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide Financial, said if the Fed skips a hike in December, they would be accused of putting a floor under stock prices - in other words, "a Fed put" - a charge that has dogged the central bank since the late 1980s.

How bad would the stock-market selloff does have to get before the Fed changes their thinking about interest rates?

Officials will keep an eye on bank distress and distress in the plumbing of financial markets as signs that there may be more trouble lurking, Anderson said.

For now, a hike in December is seen as a done deal given the hot October inflation readings. After that, the future direction of the Fed becomes more of an open question.

Concerns about financial conditions seem to favor a gradual pace of hikes, meaning the Fed pausing at its January meeting and hiking again in March, wrote Michael Gapen, chief U.S. economist at Morgan Stanley, in a note to clients.

Many economist have penciled in a more aggressive rate path, with the Fed hiking three times - in December, January and March, before pausing to assess conditions. Shenfeld said he expects two hikes, one next month and another in January.

"I think they are worried about inflation getting ingrained at 3% as opposed to 2%, which is why they are willing to put a bit of a dent into growth to pull inflation down," Shenfeld said.

A modest slowdown in growth coupled with lower oil prices could take a lot of the wind out of inflation, he added.

Some economists are worried that the Fed will overtighten, and are blinded by concern that they haven't hit their 2% inflation target in almost six years.

"Markets are signaling that the current level of interest rates is unsustainably high," wrote Andrew Hollenhorst, U.S. chief economist at Citi, who is one of the most dovish economists on Wall Street.

A rate hike remains likely early next month, but then the Fed will stay on hold and eventually cut later next year, he said in a note to clients.

-Greg Robb

data.title: AM Best Downgrades Credit Ratings of CICA Life Insurance Company of America
data.description:
AM Best Downgrades Credit Ratings of CICA Life Insurance Company of America

AM Best has downgraded the Financial Strength Rating (FSR) to B+ (Good) from B++ (Good) and the Long-Term Issuer Credit Rating (Long-Term ICR) to “bbb-” (Good) from “bbb+” (Good) of CICA Life Insurance Company of America (CICA) (Denver, CO). In addition, AM Best has revised the outlook of the FSR to negative from stable, while the outlook of the Long-Term ICR is negative.

The Credit Ratings (ratings) reflect CICA’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as adequate, as well as its marginal operating performance, limited business profile and appropriate enterprise risk management (ERM).

CICA’s balance sheet strength is driven by its weak level of risk-adjusted capitalization, as measured by Best’s Capital Adequacy Ratio (BCAR). Driven by negative cash flow and income, the company’s statutory capital levels have declined over the past four years and have continued to decline through the third quarter of 2026. This is partially offset by strong liquidity position that is within industry averages. Liquidity is enhanced by $9.5 million of Federal Home Loan Bank lending capacity and $20 million in a bank line of credit.

These sources are a liquidity backstop with no operating leverage taken at this time. The company has a conservative investment portfolio, with most of its assets being held in investment grade fixed income. Operating performance has been challenged over the last four years due to increasing underwriting expenses from growth.

As CICA continues to grow, statutory strain is expected to limit profits. While over time, management expects performance to stabilize once these new policies begin to generate positive statutory profits, the company expects to have net income losses for the next 2-3 years. Investment earnings have been adequate and consistent over the last five years.

CICA is licensed in 43 states (plus the District of Columbia) and the company is primarily concentrated in the southern United States. CICA utilizes an ERM strategy that is appropriate for its size and scale of operations, as well as the risks carried on its balance sheet. Over the near term, CICA is expected to continue developing a more formal ERM program to match its increasing operating risks.

data.title: AM Best Removes Under Review With Positive Implications and Upgrades Credit Ratings of Obsidian Insurance Group’s Members
data.description:
AM Best Removes Under Review With Positive Implications and Upgrades Credit Ratings of Obsidian Insurance Group’s Members

AM Best has removed from under review with positive implications and upgraded the Financial Strength Rating (FSR) to A (Excellent) from A- (Excellent) and the Long-Term Issuer Credit Ratings (Long-Term ICR) to “a” (Excellent) from “a-” (Excellent) of Obsidian Specialty Insurance Company (Wilmington, DE) and its pooling affiliates, Obsidian Insurance Company (Columbus, OH) and Obsidian Pacific Insurance Company (Wilmington, DE). These companies collectively comprise Obsidian Insurance Group (Obsidian). The outlook assigned to these Credit Ratings (ratings) is stable.

The ratings reflect Obsidian’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as very strong, as well as its adequate operating performance, limited business profile and appropriate enterprise risk management.

The rating actions follow the completion of Protective Life Insurance Company’s (Protective Life) acquisition of Obsidian in November 2026, and AM Best’s evaluation of parental support and integration plans. The rating upgrades reflect rating enhancement based on Obsidian’s strategic importance to Protective Life and the anticipated financial and operational benefits of ownership by a larger, higher-rated insurance organization. Protective Life has an FSR of A+ (Superior) and a Long-Term ICR of “aa-” (Superior), with stable outlooks. Obsidian is expected to provide Protective Life with product and business cycle diversification, advance Protective Life’s business expansion strategy, and strengthen its long-term earnings diversification. AM Best expects Obsidian to benefit from Protective Life’s financial flexibility and operating scale, if needed.
